claims.claim: Data cleaning — also called data cleansing or data scrubbing — is the process of identifying and correcting errors and inconsistencies in raw datasets to improve data quality, aiming for data that is accurate, complete, consistent, and usable for analysis or decision-making.

Common data quality problems include duplicates, missing values, inconsistent formats (for example date formats such as MM-DD-YYYY versus DD-MM-YYYY), syntax errors, irrelevant data, and structural errors; typos are a common source of dirty data.

Cleaning involves standardizing formats and structures, correcting errors, consolidating or removing duplicate records, deciding how to handle missing values (replace, remove, or flag), and validating the cleaned data before analysis.
Preparing data for analysis includes resolving inconsistencies, unexpected or null values, and data quality issues, and profiling columns to understand their contents before using them.

In the big data lifecycle defined by NIST SP 1500-1, the four stages are collection, preparation, analysis, and action; preparation converts raw data into cleansed, organized information, and analysis produces synthesized knowledge from that organized information.

Garbage in, garbage out (GIGO) is the computing principle that flawed or poor-quality input produces output of similar low quality; its first known use is a 1957 syndicated newspaper article about U.S. Army mathematicians, and Charles Babbage expressed the same idea in 1864.

In CrowdFlower's 2016 survey, data scientists reported spending 60 percent of their time cleaning and organizing data, and the report estimated that up to 80 percent of a data scientist's time can be spent on such work.
IBM's data management guide cites research suggesting that preparing data and transforming it into usable forms takes between 45 and 80 percent of a data analyst's time.
Analyses and machine learning models built on dirty data can produce inaccurate, inconsistent, or misleading results; clean data underpins reliable decision-making and better model performance.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How much of a data professional's time goes to data preparation varies by survey and by role.
positions: CrowdFlower 2016 survey: 60% of a data scientist's time on cleaning and organizing data, with up to 80% estimated
IBM-cited research: 45-80% of a data analyst's time on data preparation
Later surveys for specific roles report different shares
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the figures as survey-based findings attributed to their sources and frames the idea as a rule of thumb rather than a precise law.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Terminology overlap: cleaning, wrangling, and preparation are used with different boundaries by different writers.
positions: IBM treats data cleaning and data wrangling as separate topics with overlapping tasks
NIST folds cleaning into a single 'preparation' stage of the lifecycle
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson treats cleaning as the corrective work inside the broader preparation stage and does not argue for one taxonomy over another.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft described data cleaning as 'a label on a toolbox drawer' and as 'a foundational concept'; these framings were boilerplate with no factual support and were replaced with sourced content.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the entire generated draft: the definition, common problems, cleaning steps, lifecycle ordering, survey figures, and GIGO history are now source-verified, and all examples are original.
rightsIssues: No source prose reproduced. Survey figures are re-stated with attribution. The CrowdFlower report was read via an Internet Archive capture of the original PDF because the original host is defunct.

sourceRecords.title: What is data cleaning?
sourceRecords.notes: Vendor documentation read live. Supports the definition of data cleaning, the common quality problems (duplicates, missing values, inconsistent formats, syntax errors, typos), the cleaning steps (standardization, deduplication, missing-value handling, validation), and the claim that dirty data leads to unreliable analysis and models. No source prose reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: What is data wrangling?
sourceRecords.notes: Vendor documentation read live. Supports the 45-80% figure for data-preparation time with its citation of research; used as a second, independently worded source for the time-share claim.

sourceRecords.title: Clean, Transform, and Load Data in Power BI
sourceRecords.notes: Public Microsoft Learn module read live. Supports the literacy-level claim that preparing data involves resolving inconsistencies, unexpected or null values, and data quality issues, and that profiling columns precedes deeper analysis. The module is tool-oriented (Power Query); only its concept-level objectives were used, not its tool workflow.

sourceRecords.title: The 2016 Data Science Report
sourceRecords.notes: Primary survey report. The original host is defunct; read via an Internet Archive capture (web.archive.org, 2018 snapshot) of the original PDF. Supports: respondents spend 60% of their time cleaning and organizing data, and the report estimates up to 80% of a data scientist's time can go to such work.

sourceRecords.title: NIST Big Data Interoperability Framework: Volume 1, Definitions (NIST SP 1500-1)
sourceRecords.provider: National Institute of Standards and Technology
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A government standard (September 2015) read directly from the NIST PDF at nvlpubs.nist.gov. Supports the four-stage data science lifecycle (collection, preparation, analysis, action) and the statement that preparation converts raw data into cleansed, organized information. URL aligned to the registered nvlpubs canonical (DOI 10.6028/NIST.SP.1500-1 resolves to the same document).

sourceRecords.title: Garbage in, garbage out
sourceRecords.notes: Encyclopedic reference read live. Supports the GIGO principle, its first known use in a 1957 syndicated article about U.S. Army mathematicians, and the 1864 Charles Babbage statement of the same idea. Used as background; the lesson states the principle in its own words.
